summary: Defines an RTCP Extended Report block for reporting delay metrics in real-time media applications over RTP. Endpoints can share measurements of delay to monitor and troubleshoot call quality.

eli5.summary: People on a call send each other short notes saying how long their words took to arrive, so they can tell if the line is slow.

subtitle: A new RTCP report block that tells peers how long packets take to go round trip, and how much delay sits inside the endpoint.

tldr.problem: Real-time media applications need to know how much delay their streams suffer, but RTCP Extended Reports had no standard block for reporting delay.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an XR block of type 16 that carries the mean, minimum and maximum network round-trip delay plus the end system delay, along with an SDP token to signal its use.
tldr.outcome: Receivers can use the figures to size buffers and pick a playout delay, and network managers can use them to troubleshoot.

today: RFC 6843 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2013. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 6843 adds a new block type to the RTCP Extended Report (XR) format defined in RFC 3611, for use with RTP applications. The block reports the mean, minimum and maximum values of the network round-trip delay between the RTP interfaces of two peer end systems, for example as measured with the RTCP method in RFC 3550.

It also reports the part of the round-trip delay that is internal to the local RTP system. The network metrics belong to the class of transport metrics defined in RFC 6792, and the block follows the guidelines of RFC 6390 and RFC 6792.
sections.eli5: Two people on a call can tell each other how long a message takes to go there and back, and how much of that time is spent inside their own device.

sections.title: Where the Metrics Are Useful
sections.content:
The metrics apply to RTP applications such as multimedia conferencing and streaming audio and video. Knowing the round-trip delay and its characteristics can help other receivers size their receive buffers and select a playout delay.

The same information helps network managers troubleshoot network and user experience problems.
sections.eli5: If you know how late things usually arrive, you know how long to wait before playing them. A helper can also use the numbers to find out why a call sounds bad.

sections.title: How Delay Is Measured and Scoped
sections.content:
The metrics describe the packet delay of the stream arriving at the RTP system. They can be measured at the receiving end or at the sending end of the stream.

The block refers by SSRC to the separate Measurement Information block of RFC 6776, which holds the measurement period. This block relies on that period to say what span the report covers, and it SHOULD be sent in the same compound RTCP packet. If the measurement period does not arrive in the same compound packet, the delay block MUST be discarded.

The round-trip values are typically computed from the NTP timestamp in an RTCP sender report together with the LSR and DLSR fields of the receiver report. They can also come from the Receiver Reference Time Report Block and the DLRR Report Block of RFC 3611.
sections.eli5: The note about delay only makes sense when it says which stretch of time it covers. If that time stamp is missing, the note is thrown away.

sections.title: The Delay Metrics Block
sections.content:
The block is six 32-bit words after its first word, so the block length field is 6. The block type (BT) is the constant 16. An I flag of 2 bits says how to read the numbers: 10 is an interval value for the most recent period between reports, 11 is a cumulative value, and 01 is a sampled instantaneous value. Six reserved bits MUST be zero when sent and are ignored on receipt.

Three 32-bit fields give the mean, minimum and maximum network round-trip delay over the measurement period, in units of 1/65536 seconds. If only one measurement exists, that single value SHOULD be reported as the mean, the minimum and the maximum. If a measurement is unavailable, the field MUST be set to all ones.

The End System Delay is a 64-bit field in the NTP timestamp format of RFC 5905, with 32 bits of seconds and 32 bits of fraction. It is the internal round-trip delay of the reporting endpoint, calculated from the nominal jitter buffer delay plus the accumulation, encoding, decoding and playout delay of the codec. It is also all ones when unavailable.
sections.eli5: The note is a small form with boxes for the average, shortest and longest trip time, plus a box for the time spent inside your own device. Unknown boxes are filled with all ones.

sections.title: SDP Signaling
sections.content:
RFC 3611 defines how SDP signals the use of XR blocks, and XR blocks MAY be used without prior signaling. This RFC adds a new xr-format value, delay, to the rtcp-xr SDP attribute, so endpoints can announce support for this block.

In offer/answer exchanges, the usage already defined in RFC 3611 applies.
sections.eli5: Callers can say up front that they understand delay notes, but they are allowed to send them even without saying so.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The RFC assigns block type 16 in the IANA RTCP XR Block Type Registry to the Delay Metrics Block. It also registers the new parameter delay in the registry of RTCP XR SDP parameters.
sections.eli5: The number 16 and the word delay are written in an official list so nobody else uses them for something different.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC believes the block adds no new security considerations beyond those of RFC 3611. Because the block does not give per-packet statistics, the confidentiality risk described in Section 7, paragraph 3 of RFC 3611 does not apply.
sections.eli5: The note only gives averages, not details of every packet, so it does not leak more than existing reports do.

fields.name: I
fields.desc: Interval, cumulative or sampled metric flag.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to zero by senders and ignored by receivers.

fields.name: SSRC of Source
fields.desc: The source this block reports on.

fields.name: End System Delay - Seconds
fields.desc: Integer part of the end system delay.

fields.name: End System Delay - Fraction
fields.desc: Fractional part of the end system delay.
